stem: During an isothermal expansion of an ideal gas, its internal-energy change is

rationales.A: Assumes the gas gains internal energy because it takes in heat while expanding, ignoring that for an ideal gas at constant temperature the heat absorbed is converted entirely to work.
rationales.B: Assumes the gas loses internal energy as it does work expanding, ignoring that the heat absorbed isothermally exactly offsets it.
rationales.C: ideal-gas internal energy depends only on temperature
rationales.D: Confuses internal energy with pressure, treating the two as numerically interchangeable rather than recognizing internal energy depends only on temperature.

stem: Which of the following best explains why energy is spontaneously transferred from a hot object to a cold object?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The transfer decreases the total entropy of the system

choices.label: B
choices.text: The transfer increases the total entropy of the system

choices.label: C
choices.text: The transfer violates conservation of energy

choices.label: D
choices.text: The transfer decreases the entropy of the cold object

rationales.A: Reverses the direction required by the second law of thermodynamics for a spontaneous process.
rationales.B: spontaneous heat transfer increases total entropy
rationales.C: Confuses entropy increase with a violation of energy conservation, when heat flow conserves energy while still increasing entropy.
rationales.D: Reverses the actual effect: heat flowing into the cold object increases its entropy, and because the cold object is at the lower temperature (ΔS ≈ Q/T_c for a small transfer) that increase is larger than the hot object's decrease (≈ Q/T_h), so the total entropy increases.

stem: The electric field direction at a point is the direction of force on

rationales.A: field direction is defined using a positive test charge
rationales.B: Reverses the sign convention, treating the field as defined by the force on a negative test charge.
rationales.C: A neutral object has no sign of charge, so the force on it cannot define the field direction, whereas the field direction is defined by the force on a positive test charge.
rationales.D: Treats the definition as applying to one particular particle. The field direction is defined by the force on a positive test charge, whatever the sign of the charges that create the field; the force on an electron points opposite to the field.

stem: Moving a positive charge opposite a uniform electric field causes electric potential energy to

choices.label: D
choices.text: become negative regardless of the starting value

rationales.A: Assumes moving against the field lowers potential energy, as if borrowing the sign convention from motion with a field (or gravity) rather than against it.
rationales.B: Moving a positive charge opposite the field requires positive work by an external force, so the electric potential energy of the charge increases.
rationales.C: Potential energy would stay constant only for motion perpendicular to the field (along an equipotential). Moving opposite the field requires positive work by an external force, so the potential energy changes.
rationales.D: Assumes the change always produces a negative value. Moving against the field adds energy equal to the positive external work, so the potential energy rises from whatever it was; the sign of the final value depends on the starting value and the reference point.

stem: Two identical positive point charges are placed on a horizontal line, one to the left of the other. At the midpoint between them, the electric field is

rationales.A: The two charges are equal in magnitude and equidistant from the midpoint, so the electric field each produces there has equal magnitude. Because both charges are positive, each field points away from its own charge, meaning the two fields point in opposite directions at the midpoint. Equal-magnitude, opposite-direction vectors sum to zero, giving a net field of zero.
rationales.B: Accounts only for the right charge's field at the midpoint (which points toward the left), ignoring the left charge's opposing contribution.
rationales.C: Accounts only for the left charge's field at the midpoint (which points toward the right), ignoring the right charge's opposing contribution.
rationales.D: The midpoint is a finite distance from both charges, so each field is finite and the two fields cancel.

stem: Immediately after an uncharged capacitor is connected through a resistor to a battery, the capacitor behaves approximately like

choices.label: D
choices.text: a resistor with the same resistance as the series resistor

rationales.A: Describes the capacitor's long-time steady-state behavior, once it is fully charged and blocks current, rather than its initial state.
rationales.C: Assumes the capacitor starts fully charged and able to supply voltage, the opposite of its actual initial uncharged state.
rationales.D: Treats the capacitor as additional resistance that limits the current. At the first instant the uncharged capacitor has zero potential difference, so it adds no opposition and the current is set by the resistor alone, battery voltage divided by R.

stem: At a point where electric potential is zero, the electric field

rationales.A: This confuses a potential reference value with zero potential change.
rationales.B: Zero potential at one point says nothing about whether the field is uniform. The field is set by how quickly the potential changes with position, and that can differ from point to point near the zero-potential point.
rationales.C: Potential value can be zero while its spatial change, and hence electric field, is nonzero.
rationales.D: Electric-field direction depends on the spatial decrease of potential, not on whether the potential value at one point is zero.

stem: An electron accelerated from rest through a potential difference of magnitude ΔV gains kinetic energy equal to

rationales.A: The kinetic-energy gain magnitude is |qΔV|=eΔV, by the work-energy theorem applied to the electric force.
rationales.B: This incorrectly carries the 1/2 from the kinetic-energy expression (1/2)mv² into the answer; the work-energy theorem already gives the full eΔV as the energy gained, without an extra factor of 1/2.
rationales.C: This introduces an unnecessary factor of two. The magnitude of the electric potential-energy change is |q|ΔV = eΔV, and by conservation of energy that equals the kinetic energy gained.
rationales.D: This is the signed potential-energy change, not the kinetic-energy gain. The electron (q = −e) moves to higher potential, so ΔU = qΔV = −eΔV; conservation of energy gives ΔK = −ΔU = +eΔV, and kinetic energy gained from rest cannot be negative.

stem: A capacitor in series with a resistor has been connected to a DC battery for a very long time. The circuit current is

rationales.A: This describes the instant just after connecting an initially uncharged capacitor.
rationales.B: At long time the capacitor is fully charged and behaves as an open circuit, so current is zero.
rationales.C: Infinite current is impossible here: the series resistor limits the current to at most V/R even if the capacitor were treated as a short, and at long times the fully charged capacitor blocks DC current rather than shorting it.
rationales.D: This ignores that capacitance affects the transient time, not the final DC current.
